newsitem.title: JAPAN: JAL's half-year profit hit by higher fuel prices.
newsitem.headline: JAL's half-year profit hit by higher fuel prices.

text.p: Japan's biggest airline company revealed a plunge in its half-year profits on Wednesday and blamed higretreat against the dollar for the slump.

Japan Airlines Co Ltd (JAL) posted parent current profit of 5.09 billion yen ($44.7 million) in the half-year ended September 30, down 60.7 percent from the same period a year ago. Sales rose 6.9 percent from a year ago to 600.08 billion yen ($5.26 billion).
Current profit is pretax and includes gains or losses on non-operating activities, such as investment in stocks.

"Although we posted the highest half-year sales ever, the rise in operational costs, mainly higher fuel prices, resulted in the decline in profit," managing director Jiro Sagara told a news conference.

Fuel costs rose by 14.6 billion yen ($128 million) from a year ago, the company said in a statement. The price of international benchmark Brent crude oil has risen by about 28 percent since the beginning of this year.
Profits were also hit by the drop in the yen.

Airlines pay for imported fuel and aircraft replacement parts in dollars, so a weaker yen hurts their earnings by making the prices of these more expensive. A weak yen also makes travelling overseas less attractive for the Japanese, as it makes costs abroad more expensive in terms of yen.
Meanwhile Japan Air System Co Ltd (JAS), a smaller airline, was able to offset a rise in costs by launching new domestic flights.
JAS, the third largest carrier, saw its parent current profit rise 44.1 percent from a year ago to 5.0 billion yen ($43.8 million) and sales grow 8.9 percent to 165.8 billion yen ($1.45 billion).
"The major reason for our profit increase in the six months to September 30 was that we began operating many new routes," a spokesman said, adding JAS inaugurated 14 new domestic routes.
Japan's second largest airline company and largest domestic carrier, All Nippon Airways Co Ltd (ANA), is due to announce its half-year earnings results on Thursday.
Meanwhile, the airlines are facing the prospect of growing competition in the domestic market.

Discount air ticket agency H.I.S. Co Ltd said earlier this month that it plans to start operating domestic flights in two to three years' time. It would become the first challenger in the Japanese domestic market in more than four decades.

JAL also revised downward its forecast for full-year results on Wednesday. It now expects to break even on the parent current level, compared to its previous forecast of five billion yen ($43.8 million) profit.
The latter half of the business year does not include as many high seasons for vacations as the first half, officials at the airline companies said.
The JAS spokesman also said higher oil prices the yen's retreat may affect the company's full-year earnings.
"The yen is falling and there are uncertainties over the oil prices," he said.
